**Young:** control and 5hrs \ 

**Aged:** control and 5hrs \

```{r shapiro2, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
hist(as.numeric(count_x[1, 2:10]), main = "Histogram of Gene 1 Expression", xlab = "Expression")
#Only select the columns that are actually numeric
```

We’re looking at what’s likely raw or nearly raw counts, the values are very high (in the millions), and the distribution is wide and irregular. This is what **unnormalized** RNA-seq data typically looks like.

This is why we often use transformations like log2(x+1), TPM, or variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) before applying parametric statistical tests

**Why it's important**

Raw counts:

- Are influenced by sequencing depth
- Don’t have comparable distributions across samples
- Need to be normalized before comparing gene expression across conditions

>Even if this gene has values around 2 million in all samples, we can’t say whether it’s 'highly expressed' or 'differentially expressed' without normalizing and comparing across the full dataset.

::: boxy
The data is not normalized. \

# Differential Gene Expression Analysis (DGE or DEG)

Before performing differential gene expression analysis, it's important to run a few **sanity checks** on the data to ensure **quality and consistency**.

The first step is to construct the **DESeqDataSet (DDS) object**, which organizes the count data and experimental design in a format compatible with DESeq2

## Making a DDS object

DDS object belongs to the package **DESeq2**; it consists of a count matrix and a table of sample information called coldata. The design indicates how to model the samples; here, we want to measure the effect of the ages in different conditions. The two-factor variables, Age and Condition, have been merged into Group.

- First, define the sample IDs from your metadata
- Check if all sample IDs are in the count matrix
- Subset the count matrix to only include the sample columns
- Run DESeqDataSetFromMatrix

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Warning:</strong> Make sure your column names match exactly, or the code may fail.
</div>

## Matching Counting File and Sample Data


```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=T}
colnames(samples_info)    
colnames(count_x)
samples_info$Sample_name
```

## Fixing Counting File

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=TRUE}

namec <- c("gene_id", "Y_control_1", "Y_control_3", "Y_5H_1", "Y_5H_2", "Y_5H_3", "A_control_2", "A_control_3", "A_5H_1", "A_5H_2", "A_5H_3")
filter_count <- count_x[, namec]
```

## Transform matrix

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=TRUE}
count_mat_wo <- filter_count %>% 
  column_to_rownames(., var = "gene_id") %>% #This moves the gene_id column to become row names, which is the structure DESeq2 expects for its count matrix
  as.matrix()
```

## Making a comparison group

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=TRUE}
samples_info$Group <- factor(paste0(samples_info$Condition, '_', samples_info$Age))
```

## DDs Object

```{r DDs, echo=TRUE, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = count_mat_wo, # Count matrix
  colData = samples_info, #  - indicate what the design matrix is
  design = ~ Group) # - and then what column that 'splits' the data
dds
```

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> You should always navigate in your data to understand it better, you can try the code below.
</div>

```{r datainspection, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
nrow(dds)
all.equal(rownames(dds), rownames(count_mat_wo))
```


::: boxy
## 🧬 dds in DESeq2


The object dds created by DESeqDataSet() or DESeqDataSetFromMatrix() is an S4 object of class DESeqDataSet.

This is different from typical data frames or lists in R, and so the ways to access its components also differ.

**🔧 Why the difference?**

S4 objects like `dds` are structured with **slots**, and you use `@` to access these.

The `$` operator works only on **list-like objects**, and `colData(dds)` behaves like a `DataFrame`, so `$` is appropriate for accessing sample metadata columns.


**🧠 Summary**

| You want to access...                       | Use | Example         |
| ------------------------------------------- | --- | --------------- |
| A slot like count data or design formula    | `@` | `dds@design`    |
| A sample column like treatment or timepoint | `$` | `dds$condition` |


:::


## Pre-filtering

While it is not necessary to pre-filter low-count genes before running the DESeq2 functions, there are two reasons which make pre-filtering useful: by removing rows in which there are very few reads, we reduce the memory size of the DDS data object, and we increase the speed of count modelling within DESeq2. It can also improve visualizations.

Here, we perform pre-filtering to keep only rows with a count of at least 10 for a minimal number of samples. The count of 10 is a reasonable choice for bulk RNA-seq. A recommendation for the minimal number of samples is to specify the smallest group size, e.g. If there are no discrete groups, one can use the minimal number of samples where non-zero counts would be considered interesting. One can omit this step entirely and rely on the independent filtering procedures available in results(), either IHW or Genefilter. 


### Filtering low-count genes out

**Genes that are not expressed (i.e., count < 10) in at least one sample**

```{r filtering = F, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
smallestGroupSize <- 1 
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize
dds <- dds[keep,]
table(keep)
```


### Factor order and reference

**🔹 What does factor() mean in R?**

In R, a factor is a data structure used for categorical variables, like group labels, treatment conditions, or timepoints. It stores levels with a defined order, which is **critical for statistical modeling**.

**Why it's important:**

Factors are used in modeling functions like DESeq() to define experimental design.

The order of factor levels determines:

- The reference level (baseline group) for comparisons.
- How contrasts are calculated.

::: boxy

Why this matters:

DESeq2 will compare every other group to the first one ("control_young") by default.

If you don't sort the levels, R might choose an alphabetical reference (e.g., "cae5H_aged"), leading to unintended contrasts.

Setting levels explicitly avoids confusion and ensures reproducibility.
::: 

```{r refactoring = F, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

dds$Group <- factor(dds$Group, 
                    levels = c("control_young", #will be the reference level
                               "cae5H_young", 
                               "control_aged", 
                               "cae5H_aged"))
filtered_count <- counts(dds)
```

  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> You can save the new count file, you can try the code below.
</div>


## Exploratory

In this section, we strictly **do not run** any quantitative analyses or statistical tests. It is a **QC of the counts**. We are running a correlation to check gene count similarity between samples. We are running distance-based clustering and PCA to estimate the similarity between samples. It should give us an idea of the variation within sample groups and detect possible **outliers** or **mislabelled** samples.

### Distribution of expression  

The goal of this step is to understand the profile of the genes Normally-distributed by sample.

NOTE:  DESeq2 doesn’t use normalized counts; it uses the raw counts and models the normalization inside the Generalized Linear Model (GLM). These normalized counts will be helpful in the downstream visualization of results. Still, they **cannot be used as input to DESeq2** or other tools that perform differential expression analysis using the negative binomial model.

::: boxy

Before performing comparisons we need to **normalize** and **transfor** the data.

### 🔁 Normalization vs. Transformation (Conceptual)

| **Concept**      | **What it does**                                            | **Goal**                    |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Normalization    | Adjusts for technical biases (e.g., sequencing depth)       | Make samples comparable     |
| Transformation   | Changes data scale (e.g., log or variance-stabilizing)      | Stabilize variance, make data suitable for visualization or clustering |


**Normalization** makes count data comparable across samples (horizontal operation).

**Transformation** makes data easier to work with within samples (vertical operation), especially for visualizations or clustering.

:::

## Estimate Size Factors: Data Normalization

**🧪 What are size factors?**

In DESeq2, size factors correct for differences in library size (i.e., sequencing depth) between samples.

For example:

- Sample A might have 10 million reads.
- Sample B might have 20 million reads.

Even if they express the same genes equally, raw counts in B will look artificially higher.

So, size factors normalize for that imbalance, allowing fair comparisons between samples.


```{r, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE}
dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)
```

## Distribution 

- Get normalized counts (median of ratios normalization)

For each sample, DESeq2 calculates a size factor.
Size factors represent how much each sample should be scaled to account for sequencing depth and other biases.
Then raw counts are divided by these size factors to get normalized counts.

- Convert to long format
- Add sample information
- Transform the data and plot


```{r pca, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}

normalized_counts <- counts(dds, 
                            normalized = TRUE) #returns counts adjusted for sequencing depth and library size by dividing raw counts by size factors

counts_norm <- reshape2::melt(normalized_counts, 
                              varnames = c("gene_id", "Sample_name"), 
                              value.name = "counts")

counts_norm <- inner_join(counts_norm, 
                          as.data.frame(colData(dds)), 
                          by = "Sample_name")

ggplot(counts_norm, 
       aes(x = Sample_name, 
           y = log2(counts + 1))) +
  geom_boxplot()

```


<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> You can make the plot more beautiful, you can try the code below.
</div>

```{r dist-norm-expression2, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
cols_condition <- c("control" = "#264D59", "cae5H" = "#8B4513")


counts_norm <- inner_join(x = counts_norm, 
                          y = as.data.frame(dds@colData), 
                          by = 'Sample_name')


distribution <- ggplot(data = counts_norm, 
                       aes(x = reorder(Sample_name, Condition, na.rm = TRUE), 
                           y = log2(counts + 1))) +
  theme_pubr(border = TRUE) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(counts_norm$Condition.x))) +
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("sample_name") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols_condition)

distribution


#ggsave("Results/00_Distribution.png", distribution, width = 8.0, height = 5.5)

```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> Do not use normalized data as input to Deseq2.
</div>


### Sample Correlation

It’s a good idea to start by checking how similar your RNA-seq samples are to each other.

RNA-seq data often shows **high correlation between replicates** (typically R² > 0.9), especially after applying transformations that stabilize variance across the count range.

Before assessing pairwise correlation or clustering samples, we apply a **variance-stabilizing transformation** using DESeq2.

**vst()** transforms the count data to make variance roughly independent of the mean, similar to a log2 scale. It helps visualize data and perform distance-based clustering like heatmaps or PCA.
For more details, see the DESeq2 vignette [DESeq2](https://bioc.ism.ac.jp/packages/2.14/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/beginner.pdf)


**We will:**

- Apply the variance stabilizing transformation (vst)
- Compute distances between samples
- Label samples for clarity
- Visualize the correlation using a heatmap


```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
vsd <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds, blind = TRUE)

sampleDists <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))
sampleDistMatrix <- as.matrix(sampleDists)

rownames(sampleDistMatrix) <- paste(vsd$Sample_name, 
                                    vsd$Age, 
                                    vsd$Condition, 
                                    sep = "-")

pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix)

```

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> You can make the plot more beautiful, you can try the code below.
</div>


```{r correlation, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}

mat_vst <-assay(vsd)
colours = colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")))(255)

correlation <- pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix, 
                        trace="none", 
                        col=colours)
correlation

#ggsave("/Results/01_HeatMap_rlog.png", d, width = 8.0, height = 5.5)

```


<div class="extra">
  <strong>💡 Extra:</strong> VST transformation.The transformations implemented in DESeq2, vst and rlog, compute a variance stabilizing transformation which is roughly similar to putting the data on the log2 scale, while also dealing with the sampling variability of low counts. It uses the design formula to calculate the within-group variability (if blind=FALSE) or the across-all-samples variability (if blind=TRUE). It does not use the design to remove variation in the data. It therefore does not remove variation that can be associated with batch or other covariates (nor does DESeq2 have a way to specify which covariates are nuisance and which are of interest).
</div>

### 🧬 PCA on Normalized & Transformed Data

After **normalization** and **transformation**, we can explore sample relationships using **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**. PCA reduces the complexity of high-dimensional data by projecting samples into two dimensions, based on the components that explain the most variation.

By visualizing the first two **principal components (PC1 and PC2)**, we can:

- Identify **sample clusters**, **outliers**, or **batch effects**
- Evaluate whether biological conditions separate as expected
- Check if normalization successfully removed technical variation

We’ll use the `vsd` object, which contains the data after both **normalization** and **variance-stabilizing transformation** via DESeq2’s `vst()` function.

<div class="note">
<strong>📘 Note:</strong> For an intuitive explanation of PCA, check out [this interactive demo](http://setosa.io/ev/principal-component-analysis).
</div>


**🛠️ PCA Plot in Two Step**

- 1. Run PCA and extract results:

```{r PCAa, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
pca_data <- plotPCA(vsd, 
                    intgroup = c("Condition", "Age"), 
                    returnData = TRUE)

```



```{r PCAb, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(pca_data, aes(x = PC1, 
                     y = PC2, 
                     color = Age, 
                     shape = Condition)) +
  geom_point()

```

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> You can make the plot more beautiful, you can try the code below.
</div>

```{r PCAc, eval = F, echo = T, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
cols_condition <- c("Control" = "#264D59", "cae5H" = "#8B4513")
cols_aged <- c("young" = "#003366", "aged" = "#B70404")

topVarGenes_p <- head(order(rowVars(assay(vsd)), 
                            decreasing=TRUE), 
                      500)

a <- plotPCA(vsd, 
             intgroup = c('Sample', 'Condition', 'Age'), 
             returnData = TRUE)

# By condition
teste <- plotPCA(vsd, "Age", "Condition")
teste$labels

#teste$labels 
# PC1 75 %
# PC2 7 %

PCAPlot <-ggplot(a, aes(x = PC1, 
                        y = PC2, 
                        color = Age, 
                        shape = Condition)) + 
  geom_point(size = 4) +
               geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 'dashed', alpha = 0.3) + 
               geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 'dashed', alpha = 0.3) +
               scale_shape_manual(values=c(15,17,19)) +
               theme_pubr(border = TRUE) +
               theme(axis.text=element_text(size=14), 
                     axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5), 
                     axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18),
                     legend.text=element_text(size=14), 
                     legend.title=element_text(size=0),
                     legend.position="bottom",
                     axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18), 
                     strip.text.x = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")) +
              labs(x="PC1: 75% variance", y = "PC2: 7% variance", element_text(face = "bold")) +
              scale_color_manual(values = cols_aged)
PCAPlot

#ggsave("/Results/03_PCAPlot.png", PCAPlot, width = 8.0, height = 5.5)
```


### 🚨 Detecting Outliers in PCA

Outliers can distort statistical models and mask true biological patterns. In PCA, **outliers may appear as samples that are far from the main clusters**, indicating potential issues like:

- **Sample mislabeling**
- **Sequencing or library preparation errors**
- **Strong biological deviations**

It’s a good practice to run an **unsupervised PCA** on the transformed data matrix and **visually inspect** the results to catch any problematic samples early. 


We use the `prcomp()` function on the **transposed matrix** (`t(mat_vst)`) because PCA expects **samples as rows** and **genes as columns**.


<div class="note">
<strong>📘 Note:</strong> DESeq2 does account for outliers—but there are very good reasons to look for them manually.
</div>

::: boxy
- DESeq2 uses Cook’s distance to detect gene-level outliers in individual samples.

- If it finds a sample that is driving a gene’s expression to behave unusually, it:

-- Replaces that sample’s value with an imputed value (if you have ≥7 replicates).

-- Or removes the gene from testing for that contrast (if <7 replicates).

This helps reduce false positives caused by technical anomalies.
This process is automatic and happens during model fitting (DESeq() step).

**So why check for outliers beforehand?**

Because not all outliers are at the gene level, some affect **entire samples**.
:::

## Differential expression analysis with DESeq2


The final step in the differential expression analysis workflow is fitting the raw counts to the negative binomial (NB) model and performing the statistical test for differential expressed genes. In this step we essentially want to determine whether the mean expression levels of different sample groups are significantly different.


::: boxy
design = ~ Age + Condition + Age:Condition
::: 

This tells DESeq2 what factors to include in the model:

- **Age**: main effect of age
- **Condition**: main effect of condition (e.g. control vs treatment)
- **Age:Condition**: interaction between age and condition (i.e., how condition effect changes depending on age)

This model allows you to test not only the main effects but also whether treatment affects young and aged differently.

::: boxy
**What does the interaction mean biologically?**

- If the interaction term is significant for a gene, it means that the difference in gene expression between Conditions varies depending on the Age group. For example, a gene might be upregulated by Condition A compared to Condition B only in older samples but not in younger samples.

- If the interaction is not significant, it suggests the effects of Age and Condition are additive and independent — the influence of Condition on gene expression is consistent across Age groups.
:::


#### Running DEG analysis

Here, we ask five different questions:

::: boxy
**Res1** The effect of treatment in Young (the main effect) \

**Res2** The effect of treatment in Aged \

**Res3** What is the difference between Aged and Young-type without treatment (Control) \

**Res4** With treatment, what is the difference between Aged and Young? \

**Res5** Is the effect of treatment different across Ages? \
:::

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Warning:</strong>Do not use the normalized data to perfrom DEG, or the code may fail.
</div>


The DESeq2 model internally corrects for library size, so transformed or normalized values such as counts scaled by library size should not be used as input.
 
Note: In order to benefit from the default settings of the package, you should put the variable of interest at the end of the formula and make sure the control level is the first level.
 
It is absolutely critical that the columns of the count matrix and the rows of the column data (information about samples) are in the same order. DESeq2 will not make guesses as to which column of the count matrix belongs to which row of the column data, these must be provided to DESeq2 already in consistent order.


We're making a new DDS file, to make sure that cleaned all the new variables added before.

```{r lfcShrink, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
dds2 <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = count_mat_wo, 
  colData = samples_info, 
  design = ~ Age +Condition +Age:Condition)
dds2

########################FILTER THE DDS Object########################
smallestGroupSize <- 1
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds2) >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize
dds2 <- dds2[keep,]
table(keep)
########################Factor order##############################
# Set reference level for Age to "young"
dds2$Age <- relevel(dds2$Age, ref = "young")

# Set reference level for Condition to "control"
dds2$Condition <- relevel(dds2$Condition, ref = "control")

###################### Design ###############################
design(dds2) 
```

### DE Analysis Function

The function works in way to optimize the time of the analysis, it is just a loop. It can also provide a Bar Plot of the top gene.

```{r function_contrast, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

#################################################################
#### DE ANALYSIS FUNCTION ####
#################################################################
analyze_contrast <- function(dds, contrast, alpha = 0.05, lfcThreshold = 1) {
  res <- results(dds, contrast = contrast)
  ix <- which.min(res$padj)
  res <- res[order(res$padj),]
  print(kable(res[1:5,-(3:4)]))
  bar_res <- barplot(assay(dds)[ix,], las = 1.5, main = rownames(dds)[ix])
  resSig <- subset(res, padj < alpha)
  print(summary(resSig, alpha = alpha, na.last = NA))
  merged_df <- merge(as.data.frame(res), filter_count, by = 0, all.x = TRUE, row.names = TRUE)
  df_res_for_plot <- merge(as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = contrast, alpha = alpha, lfcThreshold = lfcThreshold)), filter_count, by = 0, all.x = TRUE, row.names = TRUE)
  return(list(
    res = res, 
    bar_res = bar_res, 
    merged_df = merged_df, 
    df_res_for_plot = df_res_for_plot,
    resSig = resSig
  ))
}
```

## GSEA

fgsea is an R-package for fast preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). This package allows to quickly and accurately calculate arbitrarily low GSEA P-values for a collection of gene sets. P-value estimation is based on an adaptive multi-level split Monte-Carlo scheme. 

GSEA assumes you use as input all genes in your data set, that are ranked on e.g. signed log p-value, and the algorithm then identifies which gene sets are enriched at the top (and bottom) of your ranked list. You may interpret this as gene sets being activated and suppressed, respectively, by your treatment compared to the reference.

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

res2 <- df_res_for_plot_1 
res2$Row.names <- res2$Row.names
dge_df <- res2

# First let's create a mapped data frame we can join to the differential
# expression stats
dge_mapped_df <- data.frame(
  gene_symbol = mapIds(
    # Replace with annotation package for the organism relevant to your data
    org.Mm.eg.db,
    keys = dge_df$Row.names,
    # Replace with the type of gene identifiers in your data
    keytype = "ENSEMBL",
    # Replace with the type of gene identifiers you would like to map to
    column = "SYMBOL",
    # This will keep only the first mapped value for each Ensembl ID
    multiVals = "first"
  )
) %>%
  # If an Ensembl gene identifier doesn't map to a gene symbol, drop that
  # from the data frame
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(gene_symbol)) %>%
  # Make an `Ensembl` column to store the rownames
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Ensembl") %>%
  # Now let's join the rest of the expression data
  dplyr::inner_join(dge_df, by = c("Ensembl" = "Row.names"))


```

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
  dplyr::filter(gene_symbol %in% dup_gene_symbols) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(gene_symbol)
```

### Ranking signed log and p-value 

Sort so that the highest absolute values of the log2 fold change are at the top.  \

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
filtered_dge_mapped_df <- dge_mapped_df %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(abs(log2FoldChange))) %>%
  # Filter out the duplicated rows using `dplyr::distinct()`
  dplyr::distinct(gene_symbol, .keep_all = TRUE)
any(duplicated(filtered_dge_mapped_df$gene_symbol))
#False
```

#### Making the vector list

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Let's create a named vector ranked based on the log2 fold change values
lfc_vector <- filtered_dge_mapped_df$log2FoldChange
names(lfc_vector) <- filtered_dge_mapped_df$gene_symbol

# We need to sort the log2 fold change values in descending order here
lfc_vector <- sort(lfc_vector, decreasing = TRUE)

# Look at first entries of the ranked log2 fold change vector
head(lfc_vector)
```

### Running GSEA function

**Set the seed so our results are reproducible**

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2020)
```

**GSEA function** 

Here, we can change the parameters.\

I'm using: \

minGSSize = 10 \
maxGSSize = 500 \
pvalueCutoff = 0.05 \


```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
gsea_results <- GSEA(
  geneList = lfc_vector, # Ordered ranked gene list
  minGSSize = 10, # Minimum gene set size 25
  maxGSSize = 500, # Maximum gene set set 800
  pvalueCutoff = 0.001, # p-value cutoff 0.001 0.05
  eps = 0, # Boundary for calculating the p value
  seed = TRUE, # Set seed to make results reproducible
  pAdjustMethod = "BH", # Benjamini-Hochberg correction
  TERM2GENE = dplyr::select(
    mm_hallmark_sets,
    gs_name,
    gene_symbol
  )
)

# We can access the results from our `gsea_results` object using `@result`
head(gsea_results@result)
```

```{r, echo = T, eval = F, include=TRUE, width = "100%", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
  axis.text=element_text(size=1), 
  axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5), 
  axis.title.y = element_text(size = 1),
  legend.text=element_text(size=10),
  legend.title=element_text(size=12),
  axis.title.x = element_text(size = 1), 
  strip.text.x = element_text(size = 1, face = "bold"),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "white"),
  panel.grid.minor.y = element_line(colour = "white"),
  panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(colour = "white"),
  panel.ontop = FALSE) +
labs(x = "enrichment distribution")

#ggsave("/Results/24_Res5_ridgeplot.png", Res2_ridgeplot, width = 9.26, height = 7.77)


```
